newsitem.title: USA: US bank regulators adopt bond sales practice rules.
newsitem.headline: US bank regulators adopt bond sales practice rules.

text.p: U.S. bank regulators jointly adopted on Tuesday rules governing bank sales of government securities.

Under the new rules, a bank recommending Treasury securities to one of its customers must ensure that the securities are a suitable investment given the customer's financial situation and investment objectives.

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Federal Reserve System and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp agreed that banks should follow virtually the same rules as broker-dealers when selling Treasury bonds and similiar investments.

The new rules, issued for comment last April, arose out of the Government Securities Act Amendments of 1993. Passed in the wake of the Salomon Brothers Treasury auction scandal, the law prompted regulators to reassess existing sales practices.
The bank rules are nearly identical to National Association of Securities Dealer suitability rules, although the bank rules added a definition of "government security" absent from the NASD rules.
The rules include a separate standard for larger, institutional investors. Such customers include any entity with total assets of at least $50 million.
All banks, savings associations, insurance companies and registered investment companies also qualify as institutional customers under the rules.
For non-institutional customers, a bank is required to obtain certain information and then make a suitability determination based on the information.
For institutional clients, banks may conclude based on "reasonable grounds" that a customer is capable of making its own investment decisions, thus obviating the need for a suitability determination.
